introduction-the-economics-of-tracing.core: Tracing every request is expensive. A service at 50,000 requests per second with 20 spans each produces a million spans per second, which means terabytes per day to ship, store and index. Most of those traces are near-identical successes. Sampling keeps a representative or interesting subset, trading completeness for cost while preserving enough data to debug and analyse.

first_principles.problem: A tracing vendor bill grows to $200k per month after instrumenting every service at 100%.
truths: Rare traces are the valuable ones.

analogy.title: A security camera recording every second
analogy.story: You keep everything around incidents and a sample of quiet periods, not 24/7 high-res footage forever.
analogy.breaks: Cameras can rewind; dropped spans are gone.

check.q: Why can you sample traces but should not rely on sampled traces for exact request counts?
check.a: Sampling drops data, so counts are estimates; metrics capture every event cheaply for exact rates.

head-based-sampling-the-coin-flip.core: Head-based sampling decides at the root span whether to record a trace, typically by hashing the trace ID against a ratio (TraceIdRatioBased 0.1 keeps 10%). The decision travels in the traceparent sampled flag, and parent-based samplers make downstream services follow it, so traces stay complete. It's cheap and stateless, but blind: it can't know at the start that a request will fail or be slow.

first_principles.problem: With 1% head sampling, only one in a hundred failing checkouts has a trace to investigate.
truths: Decisions at the start are cheap.
Outcomes are unknown at the start.

analogy.title: Flipping a coin before a trip to decide whether to film it
analogy.story: Cheap and fair, but you might not film the trip where something dramatic happens.
analogy.breaks: Coins are random; trace-ID hashing is deterministic across services.

code.text:
OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio
OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1
# downstream services with parentbased_* honour upstream decision

check.q: Why use a parent-based sampler in downstream services?
check.a: So they follow the root's decision, keeping traces complete rather than recording random fragments.

tail-based-sampling-the-time-machine.core: Tail-based sampling waits until a trace is complete (or a decision timeout passes), then decides with full knowledge: keep all traces with errors, all slower than 1 s, all touching a VIP tenant, plus a small random sample of the rest. Applications send 100% of spans to collectors, and the collector buffers and decides. It captures what matters most, at the cost of buffering and routing infrastructure.

first_principles.problem: Engineers need every failed payment trace, but failures are 0.05% of traffic.
truths: Outcomes are known at the end.

analogy.title: Reviewing CCTV at the end of the day
analogy.story: Keep footage of incidents and a sample of normal hours; delete the rest.
analogy.breaks: CCTV can wait a day; collectors must decide within seconds to bound memory.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every failed payment kept; 2% of normal traffic.

check.q: What is decision_wait in tail sampling?
check.a: How long the collector buffers a trace's spans after the first one arrives before making the keep/drop decision.

trace-coherency-the-golden-rule.core: A sampled trace is only useful if it's complete. If service A keeps its spans but service B drops them, you get a trace with gaps, which can be worse than none. The golden rule: every component must make the same decision for a given trace, via propagated head decisions (parent-based), consistent hashing of the trace ID, or tail sampling on all of a trace's spans in one place.

first_principles.problem: Each service samples independently at 10%, so only 0.01% of traces are complete across all four services.
derivation: Hash **trace ID** with the same algorithm.
Route **all spans of a trace** to one tail sampler.

analogy.title: A jigsaw where each person keeps random pieces
analogy.story: If everyone keeps a random 10% of pieces, nobody can ever finish a picture.
analogy.breaks: Jigsaws are static; traces arrive from many services at different times.

check.q: If four services each independently sample 10% of spans, what fraction of traces are complete?
check.a: 0.1⁴ = 0.01%, which is why decisions must be coordinated per trace.

buffering-challenges-ram-vs-latency.core: Tail sampling holds every span in memory until its trace's decision. Memory ≈ spans per second × decision_wait × average span size. At 200k spans/s, 30 s and 1 KB, that's about 6 GB per collector. A longer wait catches slow traces and late spans but needs more RAM and delays export; a shorter wait saves memory but splits long traces. Late-arriving spans need a decision cache.

first_principles.problem: Tail-sampling collectors get OOM-killed during traffic peaks because decision_wait was set to 60 s.
truths: Some traces take longer than the wait.

analogy.title: A waiting room for parcels until the full order arrives
analogy.story: The longer you wait for stragglers, the bigger the room must be.
analogy.breaks: Waiting rooms overflow visibly; collectors crash.

code.text:
# 200k spans/s × 15 s × 1 KB ≈ 3 GB per collector → give 6 GB
processors:
  memory_limiter: { check_interval: 1s, limit_mib: 5000, spike_limit_mib: 800 }
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 15s
    num_traces: 500000
    decision_cache: { sampled_cache_size: 100000 }

check.q: What happens to spans arriving after the decision_wait expires?
check.a: Without a decision cache they may be dropped or mis-sampled; a decision cache applies the earlier decision to late spans.

the-architecture-challenge-scaling-tail-.core: One collector can't handle all traffic, but tail sampling needs every span of a trace on the same instance. The standard two-tier design: a first tier of load-balancing collectors uses the loadbalancing exporter with trace-ID routing, so all spans of a trace go to the same second-tier collector, which runs tail_sampling. Scaling the second tier changes routing, so use consistent hashing and expect brief incoherence during rebalances.

first_principles.problem: Adding more tail-sampling collectors behind a round-robin load balancer splits traces across instances.
truths: Routing by trace ID keeps them together.

analogy.title: Sorting mail by family name before delivery
analogy.story: A first sorting office sends all letters for 'Smith' to the same desk so that desk sees the whole family's mail.
analogy.breaks: Families don't move desks; scaling reassigns trace IDs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each trace lands on one sampler instance.

check.q: Why can't you put a normal round-robin load balancer in front of tail-sampling collectors?
check.a: Spans of one trace would spread across instances, so no single collector sees the full trace to decide.

hybrid-sampling-strategies-combining-hea.core: Hybrid sampling layers both approaches. Head sampling at the SDK reduces volume early (say 25%), lowering network and collector load; tail sampling then keeps all errors and slow traces among those plus a small baseline. To avoid losing rare errors to the head step, SDKs or collectors can force-keep (always sample) specific routes or error-prone operations, and adjusted counts record effective rates for extrapolation.

first_principles.problem: Pure tail sampling at 100% ingest overwhelms the collectors, but pure head sampling loses errors.
truths: Some traffic must always be kept.

analogy.title: A sieve and then a hand-picker
analogy.story: A coarse sieve removes most sand cheaply, then a person picks out the interesting stones from what's left.
analogy.breaks: Sieves lose some gems; force-keep rules prevent that for known-critical paths.

example.title: Layered setup
flow: Effective storage ≈ 1–2% of traffic, all errors on /payments

check.q: What's the risk of head sampling before tail sampling, and how is it mitigated?
check.a: Rare errors may be dropped at the head; mitigate with force-keep rules for critical routes or error-prone operations.
